https://www.dw.com/en/latvians-head-to-t.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NTl0 Latvia goes to the polls for parliamentary elections on October 3, 2026. Image: Wojtek Radwanski/AFP Advertisement Four German Air Force Eurofighter jets stand ready at Latvia's Lielvarde military air base, just 60 kilometers from Riga. The aircraft are part of NATO's efforts to strengthen Baltic air defenses on the alliance's eastern flank ahead. Germany sent the jets amid repeated drone incursions, which have put Latvia on alert ahead of the country's elections on October 3. Security fears ahead of elections Security has become one of the defining issues of this campaign — defense promises appearing on the programs of most of the leading parties in Latvia. And the Latvian public's anxieties aren't unfounded. In recent months, several drones have entered Baltic airspace. The latest incident occurred on September 15 in Lithuania, when a drone believed to have crossed from Belarus was shot down by an NATO fighter jet. On top of that there are hybrid threats, including migrant flows that Latvia and its neighbors say are being encouraged by Russia's ally Belarus to pressure the EU and test border security. Intelligence officials of several European countries, including Latvia and the Czech Republic have warned that Russia could seek to test NATO in the upcoming "months, not years." Guard on the Latvian-Russian border. Image: Gints Ivuskans/AFP "There are concerns in the West and also here in the Baltic states that Russia might be trying some further actions here in the Baltics," says Maris Andzans, director of the Center for Geopolitical Studies in Riga. "If you want to test NATO, there is no better place than the Baltic states." Near-unanimous agreement on defense Latvia elects its 100-seat parliament, Saeima, through proportional representation, meaning coalition governments are the norm. Polls currently put the centrist United List, led by Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs ahead, followed by the populist alliance Sovereign Power/Young Latvians Alliance and Latvia First led by Ainars Slesers. The center-left Progressives and the conservative National Alliance are also expected to enter parliament. Most of these Latvian parties view Russia as a security challenge. "The biggest threat is our neighbors, Russia and Belarus," says Agnese Kupca of the United List. "Our partners in the EU should understand: it is not only our border with Russia, but also EU and NATO border with aggressor." Latvia is one of the few NATO members that have committed by law to spending 5% of GDP on defense, and analysts say the country's foreign policy orientation is unlikely to change regardless of which coalition emerges after the vote as there is nearly unanimous consensus on the importance of NATO. Which is backed by their voters: according to Friedrich Ebert Stiftung (FES) Security Radar 2025 Latvians generally have a positive view of NATO. Unites List election campaign poster featuring Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs before the general election in Riga, Latvia. Image: Ints Kalnins/REUTERS Economic concerns among voters But while security policy enjoys broad agreement, the economic consequences of Latvia distancing itself from Russia remain contentious. Before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia was among Latvia's most important trading partners. Since 2022, Latvia has reduced imports from Russia and Belarus by more than 90% and introduced some of the toughest restrictions in the EU on goods from the two countries. Latvia's economy has adapted, but businesses with strong pre-war links to Russia were among the hardest hit. "This closeness to the theater of war has strongly influenced the investment climate," says political analyst Filips Rajevskis. "So the big question is how to increase the investments and grow the economy." Many Latvians reject any economic cooperation with Russia on security grounds. Sixty percent said they want Latvia to reduce dependence on Russia, according to FES Security Radar 2025. "In the current situation, it's absolute nonsense. We can't watch what's happening and still be friends with Russia," one passerby in Riga told DW. Not breaking up with Russia completely? At the same time 20% of Latvians, according to FES, favor closer ties with Russia. Calls for a more pragmatic approach towards its eastern neighbor are not uncommon in the political debates. Julija Stepanenko, leader of Sovereign Power/Young Latvians Alliance, has repeatedly argued against completely severing economic ties with Russia and Belarus. Earlier this year, it emerged that Stepanenko has received gifts worth roughly €400,000 ($470,000) from her father, a Russia-based businessman whose company manufactures construction materials, including anti-tank fortifications known as "dragon's teeth." But despite that, her party remains in second place in the polls. When DW met Lyubov Shvetsova, one of Sovereign Power/Union of New Latvians party candidates at a campaign stand just outside the center of Riga, she rejected accusations that the party is pro-Russian. "Our approach is pragmatism oriented toward the interests of Latvian business," she said. Economic pragmatism Another advocate of a more pragmatic economic approach is Ainars Slesers, former businessman and leader of Latvia First. During an interview on Latvian public television earlier in September, Slesers argued that transit of goods with Russia should continue as long as it is not prohibited by EU sanctions. His party has focused heavily on economic issues, arguing that Latvia should prioritize growth and investment over what it sees as excessive self-imposed restrictions. And this approach has found support: more than 9% are ready to vote for Latvia First, which is in third place in the polls. However, discussions about fully restoring trade with Russia are premature, party member Edmunds Zivtins told DW. "As long as the war in Ukraine is ongoing, we cannot talk about it," he said. Language and identity dividing Latvia Analysts say such parties may attract some voters who feel alienated by Latvia's increasingly restrictive approach toward Russia. Golden roofs atop Saints Boris and Gleb Orthodox Cathedral are seen over trees in the centre of Daugavpils, eastern Latvia. Image: Wojtek Radwanski/AFP The appeal is not necessarily driven by support for the Kremlin. Rather, it often comes from parts of the country's Russian-speaking minority who feel overlooked by mainstream parties and uneasy about policies such as the phase-out of Russian-language school education and the reduced role of Russian in public life. About one-third of Latvia's population speaks Russian at home. However, the outcome of these elections is hard to predict. Filips Rajevskis says many voters are hiding not only their party preference, but even their decision to go to vote ahead of elections. As Latvians head to the polls, Moscow is shaping the campaign in ways both direct and indirect: as a security threat driving support for NATO and defense spending, and as an economic and cultural question that continues to divide parts of the electorate. Linert Contact Us Contact Advertise Submit News Statement of Values Terms of Service Public Notices Browse notices Place a notice Local News Different contractor named in Boardman theft allegation By DAN POMPILI September 25, 2026 5 min read Staff photo / Dan Pompili A Boardman woman, who lives in the township’s Applewood Acres development, claims a local contractor has performed substandard and incomplete work. Shown is a patched stoop after a rail was removed. Trending BOARDMAN -- The contractor accused of taking money from a Boardman woman without completing the work is not the same man whose name and face have been plastered across local news lately. A report in Thursday's Vindicator outlines the complaints from an Applewood Acres resident who told police she paid a contractor $5,000 toward a $20,000 home-improvement project more than a year ago, but the work remains unfinished and the contractor has stopped responding to her. While that behavior matches the modus operandi of John P. Bartos III, who was arrested on multiple warrants this week and has already been convicted for doing the same thing to customers across the Mahoning Valley, the Boardman woman's complaint does not involve Bartos. Rather, the allegations are against Edward Yurkovich of Boardman, doing business as Xtreme Painting and Remodeling. The homeowner, Noel Smith, said she wants to know when people such as Yurkovich and Bartos will be held truly accountable. "At what point is it enough? There's no repercussions. The system is failing us hardworking honest people," she said. "We're stuck trying to recoup our losses and save money to have the damages fixed. It took me years to save that money. $20,000 may not be a lot to some people but it's like a million to me." The Boardman report states that Smith signed a $20,000 contract in August 2025, and the contractor she hired came to the house several times through November and completed most of the work, but the backyard and back porch work was never completed. She said multiple attempts to contact him since November have failed. Smith also told police that one of the laborers on the job told her Yurkovich routinely sent him texts making excuses for why he couldn't be there. She said Yurkovich never provided receipts for soap that should have been used in power washing her house before it was painted. She said a laborer told her no soap was ever bought or used. Smith said it shows in the work. Old grass clippings and dead spiders were painted over, in some places the brick was never painted, and some of the new paint is already chipping off. What's worse is that the crime is not technically theft. She said Boardman police told her that because she paid him to paint the house and he did, she cannot claim theft. The contract also included no clearly stated end date. Even though she was told the work would be done by Oct. 1, that's not legally binding. She said the Ohio Attorney General's office told her the complaint would likely be referred for mediation, not prosecution. The Boardman police report states Smith discovered that the same contractor had been accused of doing the same thing to a woman in Poland Township in 2023, and cites a specific Poland Township police report. The police report from the Poland incident names Yurkovich and his company. In that complaint, the resident, then 81, told Poland Township police that she hired Yurkovich for work at her Woodland Road home, with an agreement requiring her to purchase supplies and pay some labor costs. She said she paid $15,554, but over time saw less and less work being performed until the project effectively stopped. After nearly a year, she said she contacted Yurkovich asking for either a refund or the materials she had purchased. She said he promised to return the supplies but never did and then stopped returning her calls. She told police she wanted to pursue theft charges. The report states that when Poland Township police contacted Yurkovich, he denied the allegations, saying he had begun the work but the project took longer than expected because of supply shortages and difficulty finding labor. He said he had recently returned to the property but the woman told him he was unwelcome and she wanted her money back. He told police he was trying to finish another job so he could repay her by the end of the month. That was in early August 2023. In September, the woman said she still had not heard from him. The police report indicates that the Mahoning County Prosecutor's Office declined to file charges against Yurkovich and police told the woman she would have to pursue the matter in civil court. There is no online record of such a suit being filed. However, a 2021 civil suit from a woman in Boardman suggests a questionable pattern of behavior on the part of Yurkovich. In that case, a Mahoning County magistrate ordered Yurkovich to pay back at least $3,500 that the plaintiffs gave him as an advance on work he never finished. The case notes show that the homeowners contracted him to renovate a guest house, giving Yurkovich an $8,000 down payment toward a $16,250 contract. They then advanced him the $3,500, "after which no work was completed." The case notes state that the homeowners then paid another contractor $9,000.00 to do the job, and ultimately their costs amounted to about $20,500. "The defendant acknowledged no work nor supplies were provided after payment of the $3,500.00," the record states. An elderly couple in Canfield, both physically disabled, also were bilked by Yurkovich, Smith said. That couple lost more than $25,000. "I feel even more heartbroken for them than for myself," she said. "They are totally living amongst the chaos he left behind." Unlike Bartos' 44 complaints under the Ohio Attorney General's consumer complaints database, there are only two attached to Yurkovich's business, Extreme Paint and Remodeling, both filed this month. One of those was made by Smith, and the complaint number matches the one in the Boardman police report. It was filed on Sept. 16. A separate complaint was filed on Tuesday. All complaints against Bartos are filed under his former business, Gridiron Windows and Doors. There are no filings yet recorded for his current business name, Pro Windows and Patio Doors. https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text: Wes Streeting is welcomed to the Pentagon by Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary. Photograph: Manuel Balce Ceneta/AP View image in fullscreen Wes Streeting is welcomed to the Pentagon by Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary. Photograph: Manuel Balce Ceneta/AP Foreign policy Wes Streeting urges US to back Ukraine on Washington visit after Starlink row UK defence secretary trying to cool tensions and is arguing it is in America’s economic interests to support Kyiv Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor Thu 15 Oct 2026 14.09 EDT Last modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 14.36 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Wes Streeting urged the US to stand by Ukraine on his visit to the American capital and sought to cool tensions between the two countries in the wake of the Starlink row that is threatening to set back Kyiv’s war effort. The British defence secretary, giving a speech before a meeting with his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth , argued that supporting Ukraine was in the long-term interests of Washington, and a business opportunity. Taking questions after his address, Streeting acknowledged “the challenges of recent days”, a reference to the row over the sudden decision of the US government on Monday to limit the use of Starlink by Ukraine’s military. He said it was “a reminder of two things – one is that American support in Ukraine has been significant and it has made, I think, a real impact in the Ukrainian war effort. And we and the Ukrainians would feel the absence of that.” The second was that there was “an enormous opportunity for the US in terms of the support for Ukraine”, a reference to the future “defence-industrial relationship” between the countries. Streeting was speaking at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a US thinktank, before a potentially difficult meeting with Hegseth amid tensions over Ukraine, Iran and the Middle East. The two men were also expected to discuss the safety of US military bases in the UK, after an Iranian threat prompted the US to withdraw B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, and whether the two countries would come together to help Saudi Arabia, which has come under attack from Yemen’s Houthis. View image in fullscreen Streeting and Hegseth during a meeting at the Pentagon. Photograph: Nathan Howard/Reuters But it is Ukraine that is the most urgent issue. A day ago, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he felt personally betrayed by Donald Trump after the US government appeared to have throttled a version of the Starlink satellite internet service used by Ukraine’s military. Ukrainian officials have reported that the US has also threatened to cut the sharing of intelligence used by Ukraine to detect incoming missiles if it does not abandon its attacks on refineries, aimed at hurting the Russian economy. The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, meeting Zelenskyy in London on Wednesday, said the UK would stand by Ukraine. Streeting said: “There’s rarely been a more important time for Britain and America to come together.” Developing the theme, he made a direct appeal to the US audience. “The people of Ukraine are fighting for a principle that runs through the finest traditions of American political thought,” he said, which was “that a free people have a right to determine their own destiny”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion Trump has vacillated over supporting Ukraine against Russia since returning to the White House, while support among US Republicans for Kyiv has been mixed. But Streeting argued that helping Ukraine was also a matter of national self-interest for the US as well as the UK. “Ukraine may be thousands of miles from American shores, but if aggression is rewarded, if borders can be redrawn by force, if the sovereignty of nations becomes negotiable, the consequences will not remain confined to Ukraine or to my continent,” he said. The change to Starlink happened without warning at about 1am, when Ukrainian soldiers reported that terminals on drones were no longer working at speeds greater than 100mph, rendering communications inoperable. It led to a dramatic halt to mid-strike drone attacks on targets in Russian occupied territories on the frontline, and concerns about Ukraine’s ability to intercept new Russian jet-powered attack craft that are bombing its cities. Trump has been trying to put pressure on Ukraine to halt its bombing of Russian oil refineries in a desperate attempt to reduce world oil prices before the US midterm elections. He agreed to buy diesel from Russia earlier this month. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Despite video footage, Netanyahu’s office described reports of the attacks as ‘unproven allegations’. Photograph: UGC/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Despite video footage, Netanyahu’s office described reports of the attacks as ‘unproven allegations’. Photograph: UGC/AFP/Getty Images West Bank Analysis Netanyahu casts doubt on settler attack witnessed by Guardian reporter Emma Graham-Harrison in Jerusalem Assault on European delegation in West Bank exposes government’s response to violence even when those targeted represent Israel’s allies Sun 18 Oct 2026 19.39 BST Last modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 20.54 BST Share Hours after Israeli militants attacked a delegation of European diplomats, French clerics and a visiting mayor in the occupied West Bank, Israel’s leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, responded by questioning the delegation’s account of the assault. “Serious accusations require serious evidence” was the all-caps headline of a social media post from the office of the prime minister. As news of the attack spread globally there was no pledge to find those accountable and bring them to justice. Instead Netanyahu’s team dismissed video of Bernard Baudoux, the mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France, on the ground grimacing in pain and shock, photos of the smashed window of a diplomatic car, and footage of masked men threatening diplomats and activists with sticks. “These images alone do not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility,” the statement said, warning of “concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel”. The prime minister’s office went on to cast doubt on the integrity of senior French, Belgian and Polish diplomats in Jerusalem and clergy from the Catholic church who witnessed and reported the attack. “We call on the public and responsible journalists to demand verifiable evidence, reject hearsay and refuse to turn unproven allegations into a collective indictment of the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria [the occupied West Bank],” it said. Guardian footage Footage below filmed by the Guardian (no audio) shows the moments before Israeli settlers attacked the French mayor Bernard Baudoux, who was in the Palestinian town of Taybeh with a delegation of European diplomats. A second clip shows the immediate aftermath of the attack. The final section shows one group of settlers attacking the car carrying Baudoux and others. 0:36 French mayor attacked by Israeli settlers in occupied West Bank – video Verifying the details of attacks can be painstaking journalistic work, seeking out eyewitness accounts, photos and videos for confirmation. But this weekend the Guardian was in Taybeh, and witnessed the masked militants speeding up a hill in order to attack diplomats and French visitors who had spent a morning peacefully harvesting olives with Palestinians who own the groves. View image in fullscreen The smashed window of the car carrying Bernard Baudoux. Photograph: Emma Graham-Harrison/The Guardian Shortly after 1pm, they were warned that settlers had attacked Palestinians harvesting olives nearby. Keen to avoid confrontation, the group decided to leave and were approaching their vehicles as the militants closed in, masked, menacing and brandishing sticks. The Guardian filmed the moments before Baudoux was assaulted, showing him approaching an SUV with his wife and Vincent Dollmann, the archbishop of Cambrai, escorted by diplomatic security. Our vehicle pulled away, making room for the two parked by the road to follow. Moments later the settlers attacked, apparently determined not only to force the foreigners to flee but to extract a price for joining Palestinians on their land. It was clear the group contained foreign dignitaries because the cars had diplomatic plates, and Baudoux was apparently targeted for his nationality, because he was wearing his mayor’s sash of office. One of the attackers aggressively shouted “France, France” before pushing him to the ground, eyewitnesses said. Metadata from that video shows there were just 22 seconds between the last shot of Baudoux remonstrating with his attackers and footage of him slumped on the ground taken by activists in the second car. The embassy security team then helped him into the vehicle but the attack continued as they drove off. Footage filmed from the hillside opposite shows the settlers attacking the SUV as pulls away. The force of their blows smashed one of the reinforced windows at the back of the car, which can be seen intact in the first video. A photo of the crumpled pane taken minutes later in the relative safety of Taybeh shows the force of the impact. If the militant settlers had broken one of the windows next to the passengers, it is unlikely those inside would have escaped injuries. View image in fullscreen Former Israeli ambassadors and employees demonstrated outside the foreign ministry, demanding the prime minister and his government ‘Stop Jewish Terrorism. It’s in your hands’. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian Israeli authorities have repeatedly attempted to obfuscate details of attacks on Palestinians and undermine survivor or witness accounts. For the prime minister to deploy the same tactics on senior diplomats from European allies – however strained their current relationship – marks a new embrace of isolationist extremism. A day earlier the American photojournalist Heidi Levine was hospitalised after a brutal attack by Israeli militants blocking the Palestinian olive harvest in another village. Netanyahu’s office described it as an “alleged assault” and a “disputed incident” adding “the facts … remain unclear and are under investigation”. The message from the very top of Israel’s government, that the state was reluctant to impose consequences or seek justice for that attack, may have emboldened the attackers on Saturday. View image in fullscreen The protest outside the foreign ministry in Jerusalem drew a response from conservative passersby. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian There was one unprecedented response in Jerusalem, however. On Sunday, more than a dozen of Israel’s top former diplomats gathered outside the foreign ministry where they had all worked for decades for an unprecedented protest. Two former directors general, one deputy director general and a host of ambassadors held up signs calling for action on the campaign of terror by Israelis against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. “Bibi [Netanyahu], foreign minister [Gideon] Sa’ar. Stop Jewish Terrorism. It’s in your hands,” read one banner.
